  Reference for the translation catalogs, the i18n runtime, non-Latin
  and bidirectional text, and right-to-left layout. Read this before adding a
  user-facing string, touching src/i18n/, or writing a stylesheet. The mistakes
  that compile are pluralising by concatenation, translating at module load or
  at storage time, nailing a style to a physical side, comparing text without
  normalising it, and translating a string that crosses the wire to bitchat.

# Internationalization

Implementation: `src/i18n/`. Decision log: `docs/spec/ARCHITECTURE.md` section 10.

| Fact              | Value                                                |
| ----------------- | ---------------------------------------------------- |
| Languages         | 35, listed in `src/i18n/languages.ts`                |
| Source catalog    | `en.ts`, hand-written; every other locale mirrors it |
| Catalog format    | `src/i18n/locales/<code>.ts`, flat dotted keys       |
| Right to left     | Arabic, Persian, Urdu. The other 32 read as English  |
| Hardcoded strings | 0, and CI fails on the first one added               |

## The Rule

Never write a user-facing string inline. Add a key to `en.ts`, then `T("your.key")` from `useT()` inside a component, or `t("your.key")` outside React.

The catalog is what makes every string greppable, reviewable in one diff, and consistent in wording.

## File Layout

| Path                           | Holds                                                           |
| ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `src/i18n/index.ts`            | `t` / `useT` / `tPlural`, the catalog registry, the RTL policy  |
| `src/i18n/languages.ts`        | the language table: endonym, direction, script                  |
| `src/i18n/plurals.ts`          | CLDR category selection, and the forms each language needs      |
| `src/i18n/layout.ts`           | RTL helpers React Native has no logical form for                |
| `src/i18n/pseudo.ts`           | the generated `qps-ploc` locale, debug builds only              |
| `src/i18n/rich-text.tsx`       | `useRichText`, for a sentence with a link inside it             |
| `src/i18n/locales/en.ts`       | the source catalog, hand-written                                |
| `src/i18n/locales/types.ts`    | `TranslationKey` and `PluralKey`, derived from `en.ts`          |
| `src/utils/message-text.ts`    | reads and writes a stored row's key: `messageText`, `systemRow` |
| `src/utils/message-preview.ts` | the same contract for the notification bell                     |

## Completeness Is a Type

Every locale is annotated `Strings`, which is `Record<TranslationKey, string>` derived from `en.ts`. A locale missing a key does not compile, so there is no runtime fallback and no coverage threshold. Adding an English key breaks every incomplete locale at compile time rather than degrading it in front of a user.

## Writing a String

**Placeholders** are named (`{count}`, `{name}`), never positional, because translators reorder sentences and a named placeholder survives that. An unfilled one renders as literal `{name}`, so the gap shows in a screenshot.

**Plurals** go through `tPlural`, never a ternary:

```ts
tPlural("mesh.peers_in_range", count); // correct
`${n} peer${n !== 1 ? "s" : ""} in range`; // wrong
```

Selection lives in `plurals.ts`: nine CLDR rule shapes cover all 35 languages, and `plurals.test.ts` checks each against Node's ICU for every integer 0 to 2000. `PLURAL_CATEGORIES` says which forms a language needs and `catalog.test.ts` holds every catalog to exactly that set, because `PluralForms` makes every category but `other` optional, so a Russian catalog carrying only `one` and `other` type-checks and reads "5 сообщение" from five up.

**A sentence with a link inside it** uses `useRichText`. Never concatenate `<Text>` fragments.

## Translate at Display, Never at Load or Storage

```ts
const SCOPES = { tag: t("chat.scope.mesh") }; // wrong: frozen at import
const SCOPES = { tagKey: "chat.scope.mesh" }; // correct
```

Three shapes of one bug, all of which compile:

- **Module scope.** Evaluated once at import, so it holds whichever language the app started in.
- **A memo without the translator in its deps.** `useMemo(..., [Colors])` calling `t()` never recomputes on a language change. Use the `T` from `useT()` inside it and list it.
- **A row written to MMKV.** Storage outlives the language it was written in, so persisted rows carry a `systemKey` and translate on render.

`npm run i18n:audit` fails on the first two. For the third, build the row with `systemRow` (or `systemPreview` for a bell entry), which writes the key, its variables and a plain fallback together.

## Non-Latin and Bidirectional Text

**Isolates.** `interpolate` wraps every substituted value in a directional isolate, so a right-to-left name inside a left-to-right sentence cannot drag the punctuation around it to the wrong side. It first strips the value with `stripInvisibles` (`@utils/strip-invisibles`): controls, bidi embeddings, overrides and isolates, zero-width space, the word joiner and tag characters, so a value cannot close its own isolate or reverse the sentence after it. ZWNJ (U+200C) and ZWJ (U+200D) survive, since Persian spelling and emoji sequences need them; any stripping of your own must keep them too. Announced nicknames and received file names go through the same function on arrival. Nothing to do at a call site, and two things not to undo:

- Do not concatenate `t()` output with a value. Use a placeholder, or the wrap never happens.
- Do not compare or index into `t()` output as if it were the catalog string. Strip first with `stripIsolates`, the way `@utils/chat-search` does.

**Word boundaries** are not `\s` or `[.,!?;:]`. Japanese writes `。`, Arabic `،`, Hindi `।`, Burmese `။`. Match with `[^\p{L}\p{N}_]` and the `u` flag.

**Comparisons** normalise both sides with `.normalize("NFC")`. Two keyboards emit the same accented character differently, and Vietnamese and Korean bite hardest.

**Cutting text** to a byte budget uses `truncateToUtf8Bytes`, never `.slice()`. It counts UTF-8 bytes rather than UTF-16 units, and backs off a trailing combining mark or joiner, which a raw cut orphans in every Indic and South-East Asian script.

**Digits** are Latin everywhere, grouping is not. Hindi and Tamil group by lakh, Georgian by thin space, and `formatNumber` in `@utils/format` handles both. A catalog may not write its own numerals. `toLocaleString` and its date and time siblings are banned by eslint: they read the device locale, not the app's language.

**The monospace face** is for machine data only. JetBrains Mono has no glyphs for ten of the thirteen scripts shipped. The rule: a value built from a formatter or a constant may be mono, a value that comes through a catalog key is prose, number or not. `APP_VERSION` is mono, `"Version {version}"` is prose.

## Right to Left Layout

- Logical properties only: `marginStart`, `paddingEnd`, `borderTopStartRadius`. Eslint rejects every physical form.
- `textAlign` has no logical end in React Native. Use `textAlignEnd` from `layout.ts`, and `"auto"` for the leading edge.
- Directional glyphs do not mirror themselves. Use `chevronForward`, `chevronBack`, `arrowBack`. `arrow-up-right` means outward and stays put.
- A header title needs `flexGrow` as well as `flexShrink`, or it ellipsizes with free space beside it.
- `layout.ts` and `radar-view.tsx` are the two eslint exemptions. The radar is a polar plot of physical space and must never mirror.
- Direction is fixed at process start, so a right-to-left language applies on the next launch. `initI18n()` reads `I18nManager.isRTL` and the stored `frameLanguage` rather than assuming the wanted language's direction is already in force, because on a first launch it is not. `App` owns the restart notice and raises it in the language being waited for.

## What Never Gets Translated

These cross the wire or derive an identity, so a translated variant is an interop bug rather than a cosmetic one. `catalog.test.ts` enforces the list.

| Thing                               | Where                                    | Why                                                                   |
| ----------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Adjective and noun word lists       | `src/utils/username.ts`                  | Identity derivation. One peer resolves to one name everywhere         |
| Transmitted `/hug` and `/slap` text | `message-thread.tsx`                     | bitchat matches the English substrings                                |
| Slash command tokens                | `/hug`, `/who`, `/msg`, `/pay`           | The parser matches them. Translate the hint instead                   |
| Channel names and geohashes         | `#bluetooth`, cell ids                   | Protocol identifiers, verbatim inside translated prose                |
| Proper nouns                        | Airhop, Nostr, Cashu, Lightning, Tor     | "Lightning" and "Tor" are ordinary words in most of these languages   |
| Nicknames, group names, notices     | everywhere                               | User content                                                          |
| Licence texts                       | `src/data/licenses.ts`                   | Quoted verbatim                                                       |
| Terms and Privacy clauses           | `terms-screen.tsx`, `privacy-screen.tsx` | English is authoritative. The reader chrome around them is translated |
| Mint and relay error strings        | wallet, nostr                            | Authored by a remote server                                           |

## Adding a Language

1. Write the translation as a flat `{ key: text }` map plus a `plurals` map carrying exactly the CLDR categories the language uses, then:

   ```bash
   node scripts/i18n-build-locale.js <code> <translations.json>
   ```

   Key order, section markers and escaping come from `en.ts`. It writes nothing unless every key is present and none is extra, no string is empty, placeholders match English, plural categories are right, protocol tokens and proper nouns survived, and no character belongs to a script the language does not write in. The result is a normal hand-editable catalog.

2. Add one line to `CATALOGS` in `index.ts`, with its import. The picker, `LANGUAGE_ORDER`, plural selection and `catalog.test.ts` all derive from it.

3. Translate the strings the OS renders, which it picks by device language rather than by the in-app picker:

   - `ios/Airhop/<code>.lproj/InfoPlist.strings` for the permission dialogs, also listed in `project.pbxproj` and `knownRegions`
   - `android/app/src/main/res/values-<qualifier>/strings.xml` for the foreground-service notification
   - the BCP-47 tag in `res/xml/locales_config.xml`, or Android 13's per-app picker cannot offer the language

   `npm run i18n:native` fails on anything missing, extra or unwired. Run it by hand, since CI does not.

## Commands

| Command                          | Does                                                                   |
| -------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `npm run i18n:audit`             | hardcoded strings, worst file first. Also fails on frozen translations |
| `npm run i18n:audit -- --list`   | every hit with a line number                                           |
| `npm run i18n:audit -- --unused` | catalog keys nothing references                                        |
| `npm run i18n:audit -- --max 0`  | the CI ratchet                                                         |
| `npm run i18n:native`            | `.lproj`, `values-*` and `locales_config.xml` against the shipped set  |
| `npm run verify:invisibles`      | control characters and bidi overrides in source                        |

Set the picker to `qps-ploc` on a debug build to read the pseudolocale: every string accented, bracketed, and padded past the longest real translation of the same key. A screen that holds there holds in all 35.

## What Not to Do

- Write a user-facing string inline.
- Pluralise with `n === 1 ? "" : "s"` at a call site.
- Call `t()` at module scope, inside a memo without the translator in its deps, or when writing to a store.
- Use `marginLeft`, `left`, `textAlign: "right"`, or `toLocaleString` anywhere.
- Compare, slice or match text without normalising it first.
- Set translated prose in `FontFamily.mono`, or a catalog number in anything but Latin digits.
- Translate anything in the table above.
- Ship a language whose catalog is not complete.
